disclaimer: This is general guidance only and is not a substitute for advice from a qualified agricultural extension officer or plant pathologist. Citrus Canker may be subject to mandatory reporting obligations in some regions — check with your local agricultural authority. Local regulations and approved practices may vary.
description: Citrus Canker is a serious bacterial disease that causes raised, corky, crater-like lesions surrounded by a yellow, water-soaked halo on leaves, stems, thorns, and fruit. The spots look similar on both sides of a leaf. Infected fruit becomes unmarketable and may drop early. The disease spreads quickly through wind-driven rain, contact with infected plant material, and contaminated tools or clothing. It can affect most citrus varieties and spreads rapidly during warm, wet, and windy weather.
immediate_actions: Stop all pruning and movement of plant material from affected trees until the situation is assessed.
Do not move any leaves, fruit, or cuttings from the infected area to other parts of the grove or to other farms.
Immediately disinfect any tools, footwear, and clothing that have been in contact with affected trees.
Report the suspected infection to your local agricultural department — Citrus Canker may be a notifiable disease in your region.
Consult a local agricultural extension officer urgently for guidance on approved management and containment measures.
spread_prevention: Establish windbreaks around the orchard to reduce the wind-driven rain that spreads the bacteria.
Avoid overhead irrigation — use drip or ground-level irrigation instead.
Strictly disinfect all cutting tools between every tree during pruning operations.
Restrict movement of people, equipment, and plant material between infected and healthy areas of the grove.
Use certified disease-free planting material only for new plantings.
Train farm workers on proper hygiene protocols, including disinfecting footwear before entering the grove.
long_term_monitoring: Inspect trees regularly, especially young growth flushes and after rain and wind events.
Keep detailed records of which trees are infected and how the disease progresses across the grove.
Work with a local agricultural extension officer to develop a long-term management and monitoring plan.
Be aware that severely infected trees may need to be removed to protect the rest of the grove — seek expert guidance before making this decision.
Monitor any new plantings closely in the seasons following an outbreak.
